question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Sharp substernal chest pain" -> "worse with inspiration" -> "relieved with leaning forward" -> "suggestive of pericarditis" -> "high-pitched rubbing sound" -> "indicates pericardial friction rub" -> "ECG shows diffuse ST elevations" -> "consistent with pericarditis" -> "most likely cause is acute viral infection" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Substernal chest pain" -> "associated with nausea and myalgias" -> "fever of 37.3°C" -> "high pulse rate of 110/min" -> "pericardial friction rub present" -> "depressed PR interval on ECG" -> "diffuse ST elevations on ECG" -> "indicates inflammation of the pericardium" -> "most likely cause is acute viral infection" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient has chest pain" -> "pain worsens with inspiration" -> "pain relieved by leaning forward" -> "high-pitched rubbing sound on examination" -> "ECG shows ST elevations" -> "indicates pericarditis" -> "acute viral infection is common cause" -> "less likely causes include Dressler syndrome and tuberculosis" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Chest pain with specific characteristics" -> "high-pitched rubbing sound" -> "ECG findings of ST elevations" -> "suggests pericarditis" -> "acute viral infection is a common etiology" -> "Dressler syndrome is less likely due to timing" -> "most likely cause is acute viral infection" -> 85%
analysis: The patient's symptoms, including sharp substernal chest pain that worsens with inspiration and is relieved by leaning forward, along with the presence of a pericardial friction rub and ECG findings of diffuse ST elevations and depressed PR interval, are indicative of acute pericarditis. The most common cause of acute pericarditis in young adults is an acute viral infection, often following a viral illness. Other options like Dressler syndrome are less likely given the acute presentation and lack of prior myocardial infarction. Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is an acute viral infection.
